opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is one of the genuine puzzles, and I don't think anyone fully understands it. I'll give you my honest take, with the caveat that it's partly speculation.

The raw numbers are striking. A human by adulthood has heard maybe a few hundred million words. These models are trained on trillions of tokens, so we're talking three or four orders of magnitude more data. If you just looked at that you'd say the models are wildly inefficient learners, and in some sense they are.

But I think the comparison is a bit misleading, for a couple of reasons. First, humans don't start from a blank slate. Evolution has done an enormous amount of what you might call pre-training. Hundreds of millions of years of selection have shaped the architecture, the priors, the inductive biases, what we pay attention to, how we learn language at all. So when a child learns from a few hundred million words, they're really fine-tuning on top of a very heavily optimized starting point. The models don't get that. They start from random weights, so part of what the training data is doing is recapitulating something like what evolution did.

Second, the data is different in kind. Humans are embodied, they interact with the world, they get multimodal, active, causal feedback. A child pushes a cup off the table and sees what happens. That's a much richer signal per bit than passively predicting the next token of a web page.

Then there's a third piece that I find interesting, which is that the models seem to sit somewhere in between in terms of where they are on the spectrum. Once a model is pre-trained, in-context learning is actually quite sample-efficient. You show it a few examples and it picks up a new task, sometimes faster than a person would. So you could think of pre-training as a bit like evolution, and in-context learning as a bit like human learning within a lifetime. That's an imperfect analogy, but I think it captures something.

What I'd push back on is the idea that this gap is a fundamental barrier. Historically, every time people pointed to some way the models were inefficient or limited, it's turned out that scale and some fairly straightforward improvements closed a lot of the gap. Sample efficiency has been improving too. So I don't treat it as evidence that we're on the wrong path. I treat it as: we're doing it a different way than the brain does, it costs more data, but data and compute are things we can provide, and the thing that matters at the end is whether the capabilities show up. And so far they keep showing up.

r001.rationale: The response says evolution shaped humans’ architecture, priors, and inductive biases before they learn.

r002.rationale: It compares pretraining to evolution, but does not say pretraining itself occupies an intermediate position between evolution and individual human learning.

r003.rationale: It compares in-context learning to learning within a human lifetime, but does not place it between long-term and short-term human learning.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most interesting open questions, and I don't think anyone fully understands it. The gap is enormous on paper. A model sees trillions of tokens. A human, by the time they're twenty, has maybe heard or read on the order of a few hundred million words. So it looks like a factor of a thousand or ten thousand, and people take that as evidence that we're doing something fundamentally wrong.

I'd push back on that framing in a few ways. First, the comparison isn't apples to apples. Humans aren't starting from a random initialization. Evolution did an enormous amount of "pretraining" for us. The architecture of the visual cortex, the priors we have about objects and agents and language, all of that was tuned over hundreds of millions of years. If you count the bits that evolution spent, the human number doesn't look so small anymore. And then humans also get a huge stream of non-linguistic data: video, interaction, embodiment, feedback from the world. Language is only a thin slice of what a child learns from.

Second, I think a lot of the model's data is going to learning things that humans never have to learn, because we're not trying to learn all of human knowledge. A child learns one language, one culture, one small slice of the world very deeply. A model is learning everything at once, every language, every domain, and much of that data is redundant or low quality. So part of the apparent inefficiency is just that the task is different.

But having said all that, I do think there's a real residual gap. There's something about how humans learn, where you can show a person a single example of a new concept and they'll generalize from it, that models have historically been bad at. And I think the honest answer is that we've been throwing scale at the problem because scale works, and sample efficiency hasn't been the bottleneck. When you have the internet available, you don't optimize for learning from a hundred examples.

The interesting thing is that we're starting to hit the point where that matters. The quantity of high-quality data isn't infinite, and the domains where we most want the models to improve, really hard reasoning, long-horizon tasks, are exactly where there isn't a giant corpus sitting around. So I think you'll see much more pressure on the efficiency side over the next few years, and my guess is that some of that gap closes, not because we discover a magic trick, but because we start combining things: better pretraining, models generating their own curriculum, learning from interaction and feedback rather than static text.

And the last thing I'd say is, I'm wary of taking the brain as the gold standard too literally. The brain is efficient in the sense of samples, but it's incredibly slow and it took a very long time, and a very expensive process, to get here. Models are inefficient in samples but they're fast and copyable. These are different points in a design space, and I don't think the human one is obviously the one we should be aiming at.

r001.rationale: The response says evolution tuned human visual-cortex architecture and priors over hundreds of millions of years.

r002.rationale: It contrasts evolution’s contribution with human learning and discusses model pretraining, but does not place language-model pretraining between evolution and individual human learning.

r003.rationale: It mentions learning from a single example but does not place in-context learning between long-term and short-term human learning.

astra-6.text:
I think there are two things that get mixed together here. One is how much experience a human needs to learn something, and the other is how much information went into producing a human who can learn that thing.

A person can learn a new game from a few examples. A language model might have been trained on trillions of tokens before it can do something comparable. That looks like an enormous difference in sample efficiency. But the human brain isn’t starting from scratch. Evolution has done a huge amount of work to produce a system with the right structure and the right predispositions for learning. It’s hard to say how you should account for that computationally, but you shouldn’t count it as zero.

There’s also a distinction between pretraining and learning in context. Once a model has been pretrained, you can sometimes show it a couple of examples of a new task and it will pick it up. So comparing all of the model’s pretraining to the few examples a human needs may be comparing different stages of the process.

That said, I don’t think this explains away the whole gap. Humans seem to learn some things much more efficiently. They interact with the world, choose what to investigate, and get feedback from taking actions. That’s a different learning setup from absorbing a fixed collection of text. The interesting question is how much of the difference comes from that setup, how much comes from the brain’s built-in structure, and how much reflects learning algorithms we haven’t figured out yet.

r001.rationale: The response says evolution did substantial work to give humans the structure and predispositions they bring to learning.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes model pretraining from a human’s few examples and discusses evolution, but does not place model pretraining between human evolution and individual human learning.

r003.rationale: It describes in-context learning as learning from a few examples after pretraining, but does not place it between long-term and short-term human learning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are a couple of things tangled up in that comparison. One is that humans seem to learn from much less data. You can show someone a few examples of a new concept and they get it, whereas a language model might train on trillions of words. And that does suggest that there’s something about human learning that we haven’t fully captured.

But the comparison is also a little misleading. A human isn’t starting from scratch when you show them those examples. They’ve had years of experience with the world, and they have a brain whose structure was shaped by evolution. So some of what looks like very efficient learning is taking place on top of a lot of prior structure and experience.

The other distinction is between training and learning in context. Once you’ve trained a language model, you can often give it a few examples of something and it will pick up what you want. That’s a more reasonable comparison to a human learning a new task than comparing the human’s few examples to the model’s entire pretraining run.

I don’t think that completely resolves the question. Humans still seem to have advantages in how they learn continuously and how they connect experience to an understanding of the world. But I’d be careful about concluding, just from the number of words involved, that we know how large the underlying efficiency gap is.

r001.rationale: It says the human brain’s structure was shaped by evolution, identifying evolution as a source of prior structure for learning.

r002.rationale: It contrasts human evolution and experience with model pretraining, but does not place model pretraining between evolution and individual human learning.

r003.rationale: It says in-context learning is a more reasonable comparison to learning a new task, but does not place it between long-term and short-term human learning.
